stem: In a certain code, MANGO is written as NBNHP. Using the same rule, how is GRAPE coded?

per_option_rationale.rationale: Each letter is shifted forward by 1 position in the alphabet: G+1=H, R+1=S, A+1=B, P+1=Q, E+1=F giving HSBQF.
The first letter G was not shifted (kept as G instead of H), producing GSBQF instead of HSBQF.
The third letter A was coded as A (shift = 0) instead of B (shift = +1), giving HSAQF.
The pattern was mistaken for +2 shift: G+2=I, R+2=T... but the first two letters here diverge, producing IRBQF which does not match the +1 rule.

explanation: The coding rule shifts each letter one position forward in the alphabet. Verify: M->N, A->B, N->O, G->H, O->P gives NBNHP which matches. Applying +1 to each letter of GRAPE: G->H, R->S, A->B, P->Q, E->F yields HSBQF.

explanation_sections.punchline: Every letter advances by exactly one position in the alphabet - the simplest possible Caesar-type shift.
explanation_sections.approach: Deductive trace: identify the shift by comparing one known pair letter-by-letter (M->N is +1), confirm it holds for all five letters of MANGO, then apply the same +1 shift to each letter of GRAPE.
explanation_sections.lesson: Always verify the shift rule on every letter of the given example before applying it to the unknown word.
explanation_sections.timing: About 40-50 seconds. Fastest elimination: any option with G as the first letter (shift of 0) is immediately wrong.
